articles.title: How Will History Remember Conor McGregor? #ufc
articles.description: How will Conor McGregor be remembered when his fighting career is over? Chael Sonnen believes fans sometimes lose sight of just how incredible Conor was at his peak. McGregor simultaneously held UFC titles at featherweight and lightweight—the two deepest, most competitive divisions in the sport. That accomplishment alone gives him a legitimate place in the greatest-of-all-time conversation. But is that what history will remember? Chael compares Conor's legacy to Mike Tyson's, pointing out that the final chapters of a legendary career can often overshadow everything that came before. Great fighters aren't defined by one night or even a handful of performances—they're judged by the total body of work they leave behind. So where does Conor McGregor rank among the all-time greats? Is he the greatest fighter in UFC history, the biggest superstar the sport has ever produced, or something else entirely? Let us know your answer in the comments: **How should history remember Conor McGregor?** #ConorMcGregor #UFC #ChaelSonnen #MMA #GOAT #UFCHistory #CombatSports #MMAAnalysis

articles.title: 20 Years Ago Today, The WEC Named A Card After Our Founder 🔥🔥
articles.description: Twenty years ago today, the WEC named a card after a man who never fought a day in his life. He founded this site. Ryan Bennett co-founded MMAWeekly.com. Before Zuffa bought the WEC, he was its play-by-play voice. He was the guy holding the microphone in the cage after UFC 33 through 40. And every day he hosted MMAWeekly Radio alongside Frank Trigg. If you followed this sport in the early 2000s, you heard Ryan whether you knew his name or not. On May 31, 2006, he was driving his family across Utah on I-15. The vehicle went off the road. His wife and all four of his children survived. Ryan was killed instantly. He was 35. Two months later the WEC put his name on the card — WEC 22, July 28, 2006. Wes Sims was offered a bigger payday somewhere else that same weekend. He turned it down. In his own words in this video: "You can't put a price tag on friendship." Then he opened the fight with a flying drop kick — because that was the one thing Ryan had asked him for, over and over, for years. He finished it in 28 seconds. And on that same card, a young Brazilian named Glover Teixeira choked his opponent out in under 90 seconds. Fifteen years later he'd be UFC light heavyweight champion of the world. One night in a casino ballroom in Lemoore, California, for the guy who spent his whole life pointing a microphone at everybody else. If you remember Ryan, tell us below. 🤍 #RyanBennett Website: http://www.MMAWeekly.com/ Subscribe on Youtube: https://www.youtube.com/subscription_center?add_user=MMAWeeklyVideos Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/MMAWeeklycom-176775391774/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/MMAWeeklycom/ Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/mmaweekly/

articles.title: THIS DAY in MMA - JULY 27 🔥
articles.description: THIS DAY in MMA - JULY 27 🔥 2024 — Belal Muhammad walks into Leon Edwards' hometown of Manchester and takes his welterweight title. Nine takedowns in front of 17,000 people who came to boo him. 2019 — Cris Cyborg beats Felicia Spencer at UFC 240. Nobody in that building knew they'd just watched her last fight in the UFC. Six days later she was released. 2013 — Demetrious Johnson armbars John Moraga with 77 seconds left in the fifth round. His first ever finish in the Octagon, and the latest finish in UFC history at the time. 1997 — Mark Kerr makes his UFC debut at UFC 14 and wins the entire heavyweight tournament in ONE night. They called him The Smashing Machine. Almost 30 years later, Dwayne Johnson played him on screen. Same date.
